title: Throughput Target Translator and Safety Throttles for Dedicated Fleets
creator: Aisha Kapoor
description: Context: Dedicated customers require predictable throughput commitments while we retain the ability to autoscale for transient demand. Current autoscalers operate directly on raw metrics (tokens/sec, running requests). This ticket defines a translator layer that maps customer-facing SLA targets (e.g., committed TPS, p95 tail latency budget, concurrency caps) into internal scaling targets and safety throttles. Goals: map SLA -> scaling target(s), expose per-tenant safety limits, and provide configurable rollback/soft-fail behaviors.
decision_summary: We will implement a two-stage policy engine: (1) Throughput Target Translator converts high-level commitments (committed throughput, latency envelope, burst allowance) into concrete internal objectives (target_tokens_per_sec, target_concurrency, percentile latency target). (2) Safety Throttles layer enforces hard caps and surge fences (temporary deny/queue or degrade) and implements circuit breakers (headroom credits, cooldown). Chosen scaling algorithm: derivative-limited integrator (PID-lite) with explicit slew-rate limits and a budget-aware preemptive throttle when headroom is exhausted.
acceptance_criteria: 1) The translator accepts SLA objects and produces consistent internal targets returned by /v1/internal/policy/translate. 2) Autoscaler actuates changes without violating configured slew-rate limits. 3) Safety throttles prevent more than X% over-commit for a tenant and enforce per-tenant burst windows. 4) Unit + integration tests covering cold-start, burst, and steady ramp scenarios with synthetic load. 5) Runbook and dashboard panels published in Console.
notes_and_tradeoffs: Trade-offs considered: (a) Strict mapping of SLA->tokens/sec is simple but brittle across heterogeneous models; instead we map to a multi-dimensional objective (tokens/sec + concurrency + suggested model-variant). (b) Aggressive autoscaling reduces latency but increases cost; we therefore combine derivative limiting with headroom credits to permit short bursts without permanent scale-up. (c) Implementing tenant-level hard caps increases isolation but can lead to customer-visible throttles—we provide soft-fail and progressive degradation modes.
test_plan: 1) Unit tests validate translator math for a variety of SLA shapes (small/large committed throughput, tight/loose latency budgets). 2) Integration harness simulates a dedicated fleet with model mix A/B and applies load patterns: steady, ramp, step, and spike. 3) Chaos test: kill 1/3 of nodes during a spike and validate safety throttle behavior and rollback. 4) Load test against production-snapshot traffic in staging with two customer tenants (one high-priority, one best-effort).
rollout_and_monitoring: Phased rollout: feature-flagged in staging -> canary on 2 dedicated fleets -> 10% of fleets -> global. Monitoring: Console panels for translated targets, actuator commands, headroom credit burn rate, throttle events, and customer-visible latency percentiles. Alerts: throttle-rate > 0.5% over 5m for a committed tenant (SEV2), headroom exhaustion for >30s (SEV1).

Design: suggest UX for exposing translated internal targets in Console
Security: ensure headroom ledger can't be manipulated by crafted requests
